definition.text: Computer data storage is the retention of digital data using computer components and recording media.

facts.text: Faster, volatile components are generally called memory, while slower, persistent components are called storage.
In current usage, storage means devices and media the CPU cannot reach directly (secondary or tertiary storage), while memory means semiconductor read-write storage, typically DRAM.
Any text, numbers, pictures or audio can be converted to a string of bits, and the most common unit of storage is the byte, equal to 8 bits.
Compression represents data with a shorter bit string and uses substantially less storage (tens of percent) for many types of data, at the cost of more computation.
Whether to keep data compressed is decided by weighing the storage savings against the cost of computation and possible delays in data availability.
Data may be encrypted in storage so that chunks of storage snapshots cannot be reconstructed without authorization, while encryption in transit protects data being transmitted.
Redundancy lets a computer detect errors in coded data, such as a random bit flip, and correct them; redundancy solutions include storage replication, disk mirroring and RAID.
Different types of storage fail in different ways: head crashes on mechanical hard drives and electronic component failures on flash storage can cause instant total loss.

title: Storage hierarchy
article: Computer data storage#Architecture > Storage and memory

definition.text: The storage hierarchy ranks storage from primary memory, which the CPU reads directly, down through slower and cheaper secondary, tertiary and offline storage.

facts.text: Primary storage, or main memory, is directly accessible to the CPU, which continuously reads instructions from it and keeps actively used data there.
Secondary storage is not directly accessible by the CPU; computers use input/output channels to transfer the desired data into primary storage.
Secondary storage is non-volatile and is usually an HDD or SSD, with access time per byte measured in milliseconds, against nanoseconds for primary storage.
Modern computer systems typically have two orders of magnitude more secondary storage than primary storage, because secondary storage is less expensive.
Secondary storage is addressable by block and is transferred in large contiguous blocks to reduce seek time and rotational latency.
Using multiple disks in parallel, for example with RAID, increases the bandwidth between primary and secondary memory and eases the I/O bottleneck.

Tertiary storage uses a robotic arm to mount removable media and suits archiving rarely accessed data in extraordinarily large stores, though it is much slower than secondary storage (5-60 seconds vs. 1-10 milliseconds).
Offline storage sits on media that are removed or disconnected and not under a processing unit's control; unlike tertiary storage, it cannot be accessed without human interaction.

definition.text: Storage technologies are told apart by core characteristics such as volatility, mutability, accessibility, addressability, capacity and performance.

facts.text: The core characteristics that differentiate storage technologies are volatility, mutability, accessibility, addressability, capacity and density, and performance.
In random access, any location can be reached in about the same time; in sequential access, pieces are read in serial order, so access time depends on which piece was read last.
Storage can be location accessible (selected by numerical memory address), file addressable, or content-addressable.
Storage performance metrics include latency, throughput, granularity and reliability.

definition.text: Direct-attached storage uses no network, while network-attached storage and storage area networks give a computer access to mass storage over a network.

facts.text: Secondary or tertiary storage may connect to a computer over a network, but primary storage never does; direct-attached storage (DAS) is traditional mass storage that uses no network.

Network-attached storage (NAS) is mass storage that another computer can access at file level over a local or wide area network or the Internet, commonly using the Network File System and Server Message Block protocols.
A NAS is a device on the network for storing and retrieving data from a central location, and it is flexible: more storage can be added to what exists.

A storage area network (SAN) is a specialized network providing storage capacity to other computers, commonly associated with Fibre Channel; SANs once provided block-level storage and NAS file-level storage, a split that cloud services have shifted.

definition.text: Block storage divides data into blocks and stores them as separate pieces, each with a unique identifier.

facts.text: Block storage presents raw blocks to the server as a volume; the server can format them as a file system or hand control of the blocks to an application.
It is the most flexible and versatile form of storage, and databases and virtual machine engines manage blocks directly to squeeze out the most performance.
A unique identifier per block lets the storage system place the pieces wherever is most convenient, which creates multiple paths to the data; on a request the system reassembles the blocks.
Hard disk drives and solid-state drives physically attached to servers are all block storage.
Block storage can be connected over a high-speed network or protocols such as Fibre Channel and iSCSI, but conceptually it still presents raw blocks and works like attached storage.
Whether attached physically or over a network, block storage is fully owned by a single server and is not a shared resource.
A volume is a fixed amount of storage on a disk or tape; one disk can hold more than one volume, or a volume can span more than one disk.
In the cloud, block-level storage emulates a physical block device such as a hard drive; Amazon EBS is an example.

definition.text: File storage stores data as files and presents them to users as a hierarchical directory structure.

facts.text: File storage is built on top of block storage and gives a higher-level abstraction that makes files and directories easier to handle.
To locate a file in file storage, the complete path of the file is required.
It is the most common general-purpose storage solution: user-friendly, economical and easily structured, and it appears the same to the user as it does on the hard drive.

Many servers can reach file storage through file-level network protocols such as SMB/CIFS and NFS, without managing blocks or formatting volumes, which suits sharing many files and folders within an organization.
A file system format gives secondary storage the abstraction to organize data into files and directories, with metadata such as owner, access time and access permissions.
Examples are Amazon EFS, Azure Files and Google Cloud Filestore.

title: Object storage

definition.text: Object storage breaks data files into pieces called objects and stores them in a single repository that can be spread across multiple networked systems.

facts.text: Object storage keeps all data as objects in a flat structure with no hierarchical directory, unlike file storage's hierarchy or block storage's equal-size blocks.
It deliberately trades performance for high durability, vast scale and low cost, and is relatively slow compared with other storage types.
It targets relatively cold data and is mainly used for archival and backup.

Each object carries a globally unique identifier and metadata, and unlike the fixed metadata of file systems, object storage allows full custom object-level metadata for indexing, data-management policies and centralized management.

Applications use programmatic, mostly REST-based interfaces with basic create, read, update and delete functions; some implementations add versioning, replication, life-cycle management and movement of objects between storage tiers.

Object storage abstracts lower storage layers: administrators need not build logical volumes or set RAID levels, and an object can be addressed by a unique identifier within a bucket or across the whole system.

It retains massive amounts of unstructured data written once and read once or many times, but is not for transactional data: it lacks the locking and sharing mechanisms that keep a single, accurately updated version of a file.
The vast majority of cloud storage leverages an object-storage architecture, as in Amazon S3, Microsoft Azure Blob Storage and Google Cloud Storage.

notes: Overview guide S:5f5cbd733f1f lists 'Google block storage' as Google's object store; likely a slip for Google Cloud Storage, so not used.

definition.text: Object stores are used for archiving, unstructured data, cloud-native storage, data lakes, IoT data, and backup and recovery.

facts.text: For archiving, an object store can hold old data kept for auditing or client statements, a cost-effective layer of storage outside the core systems.

For unstructured and semi-structured data such as music, video and text documents, an object store fits better than the old practice of storing them as blobs in a relational database, which was quite inefficient.

Cloud-native applications get flexible, scalable storage through easy API access, and an object-store data lake gives business lines a place to dump data for later analytics, machine learning, ETL or a data warehouse.
An object store can hold IoT sensor time series for later analytics, and database or file system backups that can be loaded for fast recovery, which improves availability.

definition.text: Cloud storage is storage built on highly virtualized infrastructure, offered with cloud-native interfaces and elastic scaling.

facts.text: Cloud storage, a subset of cloud computing, has cloud-native interfaces, near-instant elasticity and scalability, multi-tenancy and metered resources.
Cloud storage services can be used from an off-premises service or deployed on-premises.
There are three types of cloud storage: object storage, file storage and block-level storage.
Instance stores are cloud-hosted block-level storage provided as part of a cloud instance; unlike other block storage, their data is lost when the instance is stopped.

definition.text: The Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) is a distributed file system designed to run on commodity hardware.

facts.text: HDFS is highly fault-tolerant, designed for low-cost hardware, and provides high throughput access to application data, which suits large data sets.
It is designed to store very large files reliably across machines in a large cluster.
HDFS stores each file as a sequence of blocks, all the same size except the last, and replicates the blocks of a file for fault tolerance.

definition.text: RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) stores the same data on multiple hard disks or SSDs to protect against a drive failure.

facts.text: RAID is a way of storing the same data on several hard disks or SSDs so data survives a drive failure, though not every RAID level aims at redundancy.
RAID is one of the redundancy solutions for stored data, alongside storage replication and disk mirroring.
Using multiple disks in parallel, as RAID does, increases bandwidth between primary and secondary memory and reduces the I/O bottleneck.

RAID coordinates two or more drives into a disk array and distributes written data across it; the configurations are called RAID levels, distinguished by redundancy, minimum drives, performance, fault tolerance and availability.
The definitive techniques are data striping, to improve read/write efficiency, and disk mirroring or parity drives, for data recovery.
Drive failures grow more frequent as drives are added, but building in redundancy lets an array's reliability far exceed that of any single high-capacity drive.
Most parity data is calculated with XOR, while RAID 6 uses a Galois field or Reed-Solomon error correction; all standard levels except RAID 1 present several devices as one logical volume.

RAID guards against physical drive failure only: data is still exposed to operator error, software, hardware and virus destruction, and the whole array to fire or disaster, so backups can be stored off site.

title: RAID levels

definition.text: RAID levels differ in how they combine striping, mirroring and parity, trading capacity, speed and fault tolerance.

facts.text: RAID 0, also known as striping, splits data evenly across all the drives in the array; it has no fault tolerance and uses 100% of capacity.
RAID 1, also known as mirroring, keeps the exact copy of a set of data on at least two drives, so if a drive fails the others still work; capacity utilization is 50%.
RAID 5 is striping with parity: it needs at least 3 drives and spreads the parity across the drives as well as striping the data; capacity utilization is 67%-94%.
RAID 6 is like RAID 5 but writes parity to two drives, tolerating a two-drive failure; capacity utilization is 50%-80%.

RAID 10 combines striping with mirroring: all data is mirrored on secondary drives and striped across each set of drives to speed transfers; it tolerates up to one disk failure in each sub-array, at 50% capacity utilization.
RAID 0 multiplies read and write throughput by the number of drives, but any one drive failing makes the whole volume inaccessible, so it is a poor choice when data reliability matters.
In RAID 1 any read can be served by any drive in the mirrored set, but write throughput is always slower because every drive must be updated; the array runs while at least one drive works.

RAID 1+0 (RAID 10) stripes across mirrored drives and survives multiple drive losses if no mirror loses all its drives; RAID 0+1 mirrors two stripes and is riskier to rebuild, as all drives of the surviving stripe are read.

notes: Singh's comparison table collapses repeated cells (the fault tolerance row has 4 values for 5 levels, write performance 4), so only the capacity row and the unambiguous ends of the fault tolerance row are used.

definition.text: Erasure coding protects data by splitting it into chunks spread over different servers and adding parities, so lost chunks can be rebuilt.

facts.text: Erasure coding handles durability differently from replication: it chunks data into smaller pieces placed on different servers and creates parities, so after failures the chunks and parities reconstruct the data.

In 4 + 2 erasure coding, data is split into four even-sized chunks and a mathematical formula calculates two parities; if two chunks are lost to node crashes, the formula rebuilds them from the survivors.
In the 4 + 2 example, every two chunks of data need one parity block, so the storage overhead is 50%, while 3-copy replication has a storage overhead of 200%.
Assuming a node has a 0.81% annual failure rate, Backblaze's calculation gives erasure coding 11 nines of durability against 6 nines for 3-copy replication.
An erasure code turns a message of k symbols into a longer code word of n symbols so the original can be recovered from a subset of the n; optimal codes need any k of the n.
Replication wastes many bytes, so increasingly large storage systems such as those in data centers use erasure-coded storage, most commonly Reed-Solomon codes.

In RS(10, 4), 10 MB of data becomes ten 1MB blocks plus four 1 MB parity blocks and tolerates up to 4 concurrent failures, at storage overhead of 14/10 = 1.4×, against 50/10 = 5.0× for full replication.
RAID is generally applied to an array attached to a single host, a single point of failure, whereas erasure coding generally implies multiple hosts, so operations continue when any one host stops.

title: Object stores versus key-value stores
article: Object storage#Differences between key–value and object stores

definition.text: An object store resembles a key-value store but adds attributes to each item and is built for large data, so the two differ in metadata, size and consistency.

facts.text: A key-value store identifies data by a key, an arbitrary sequence of bytes, rather than a block number, and its values may be of arbitrary size; the border with object stores is blurred.
Object stores resemble key-value stores in two respects: the object identifier or URL can be an arbitrary string, and the data may be of arbitrary size.
Unlike key-value stores, object stores associate a limited set of attributes (metadata) with each piece of data; key, value and attributes together form an object.

Object stores are optimized for hundreds of megabytes or even gigabytes and usually offer weaker consistency such as eventual consistency, while key-value stores expect small values (kilobytes) and offer strong consistency.

title: Parity check
article: Erasure code#Optimal erasure codes > Parity check

definition.text: A parity check appends one checksum value to k values, so any single erased value can be recovered.

facts.text: Parity check is the special case of an optimal erasure code where n = k + 1: a checksum computed from the k source values is appended to them.
If any one of the values is erased, it can easily be recovered by summing the remaining variables.
RAID 5 is a widely used application of the parity check erasure code using XOR, giving the same single-drive failure protection as RAID 1 with fewer hard drives.

title: Weaknesses of RAID
article: RAID#Weaknesses > Increasing rebuild time and failure probability

definition.text: RAID arrays can still be lost when a second drive fails during a long rebuild, when read errors surface, or when a crash leaves parity inconsistent.

facts.text: Drives in an array are often the same age and environment, so failures are correlated: in a study of about 100,000 drives, two failures within one hour were four times more likely than an exponential distribution predicts.

Capacity has grown much faster than transfer speed, so large drives may take hours if not days to rebuild; with one redundant drive (RAID 3, 4, 5 or two-drive RAID 1) a second failure loses the array.

Large RAID 5 arrays are likely to hit an unrecoverable read error on a surviving drive during a rebuild; RAID 6 survives double-drive failures at the price of a higher write penalty, and mirroring has lower risk from such errors.

A crash during a write can leave parity inconsistent with data (the write hole), so parity cannot recover a failed disk; remedies include write-ahead logging, a nonvolatile cache in hardware RAID, and a write-intent bitmap.

definition.text: Data scrubbing is the periodic reading and checking of every block in a disk array, including blocks not otherwise accessed, to find bad blocks before they are used.

facts.text: Data scrubbing (patrol read) has the RAID controller periodically read and check all blocks in an array, including those not otherwise accessed, which detects bad blocks before use.
It uses the array's redundancy to recover a bad block on a single drive and reassign the recovered data to spare blocks elsewhere on the drive.
Run as a background process, scrubbing detects and recovers from unrecoverable read errors, reducing the risk of them causing double-drive failures during a rebuild.

definition.text: RAID can be implemented by dedicated hardware controllers, by operating system software, or by firmware and drivers on a standard drive controller.

facts.text: Data distribution across drives can be managed by dedicated hardware or by software, which may sit in the operating system, in the firmware and drivers of a standard drive controller, or inside the hardware RAID controller.
Hardware RAID controllers are expensive and proprietary, and each manufacturer's own tooling for each operating system ensures vendor lock-in.
Many modern operating systems provide software RAID as a device-abstraction layer such as Linux md, a logical volume manager such as LVM, or a file system component such as ZFS or Btrfs.
Cheaper firmware- and driver-based controllers use a standard drive controller chip with proprietary firmware and drivers, so they may not work when the host operating system lacks driver support.

definition.text: Volatile memory is computer memory that needs power to keep its contents and quickly loses the stored data when power is interrupted.

facts.text: Most general-purpose random-access memory (RAM) is volatile, and volatile memory is used as primary storage.
Volatile memory is usually faster than mass storage such as a hard disk drive, and volatility can protect sensitive information because it becomes unavailable on power-down.
There are two kinds of volatile RAM, dynamic (DRAM) and static (SRAM); both need continuous electrical current to retain data.
DRAM keeps each bit in a capacitor, needing only one capacitor and one transistor per bit, which makes it space-efficient, inexpensive and very popular.
SRAM is much faster than DRAM and needs no refreshes, but each bit takes a cell of six transistors, so it cannot reach the storage capacity of DRAM.
SRAM is commonly used as CPU cache and for processor registers and in networking devices.

definition.text: Non-volatile memory is computer memory that retains stored information even after power is removed.

facts.text: Non-volatile memory is typically used for secondary storage or long-term persistent storage.
Most forms are unsuitable as primary storage: compared with volatile RAM they typically cost more, perform worse or have a limited lifetime.
Non-volatile storage is either electrically addressed, such as flash memory and read-only memory, or mechanically addressed, such as hard disks, optical discs, magnetic tape and holographic memory.
Electrically addressed systems are generally expensive and limited in capacity but fast, while mechanically addressed systems cost less per bit but are slower.
Mechanically addressed systems use a recording head: magnetic tape is sequential, since the tape must pass the head, while hard disk drives and optical discs give random access.
Mask ROMs are programmed only at the factory, PROM can be written once, EPROM is erasable by ultraviolet light but clears the whole device at once, and EEPROM erases with voltage but slowly.

Newer electrically addressed technologies include ferroelectric RAM, magnetoresistive RAM, phase-change memory and ReRAM; ReRAM was seen as a flash replacement, but its cost and performance benefits have not persuaded companies to switch.
Non-volatile main memory (NVMM) is primary storage with non-volatile attributes, NVDIMM being one example, and it presents security challenges.

definition.text: Flash memory is a solid-state chip that maintains stored data without any external power source.

facts.text: Flash is a close relative of EEPROM, but erase operations must be done on a block basis and its capacity is substantially larger.
NOR flash provides high-speed random access, reading and writing specific memory locations, and can retrieve as little as a single byte.
NAND flash reads and writes sequentially at high speed in blocks and reads faster than it writes, but it is slower at reading than NOR.
At high densities NAND is less expensive than NOR and offers higher capacity for the same silicon.

NAND cells are classed by bits per cell: single-level cells (1 bit) give the best performance and endurance at higher cost, while MLC, TLC and QLC (2, 3 and 4 bits) cost less but perform and endure less.
Many SSDs use 3D NAND, with memory cells stacked vertically, which raises storage density while improving performance and reducing costs.

definition.text: A solid-state drive (SSD) is a storage device that uses integrated circuits, typically NAND flash, to store data persistently.

facts.text: With no moving parts, SSDs deliver faster data access, lower latency, resistance to physical shock, lower power consumption and silent operation than hard disk drives.
Lower latency gives SSDs higher IOPS than HDDs; random access typically takes 0.05-0.2 ms on consumer NAND SSDs against 2.9 ms (high-end) to 12 ms (laptop) on HDDs.
SSDs are generally more expensive per gigabyte and have a finite number of write cycles, while hard disk drives offer significantly higher capacity for their price.

Every SSD has a controller, an embedded processor running firmware, that manages data flow between the NAND and the host and performs bad block mapping, ECC, garbage collection, wear leveling, caching and encryption.
SSD performance scales with the number of parallel NAND chips and the controller's efficiency, and internal parallelism lets a drive handle multiple operations at once.
SSDs fail differently from hard disks: a sudden power loss can leave incomplete or failed writes, and the failure of a single chip can lose all data stored on it.

Studies find SSDs generally reliable, with lower failure rates than HDDs but more uncorrectable errors; wear-leveling algorithms are complex and hard to test, so firmware bugs are a major cause of data loss.

Higher-performing SSDs carry capacitors, supercapacitors or batteries that supply enough power to write cached data to non-volatile memory after a power loss; enterprise drives add such power loss protection.

title: Wear leveling and TRIM
article: Solid-state drive#Architecture and function > Controller > Wear leveling

definition.text: Wear leveling is a technique that spreads write and erase operations evenly across all blocks of an SSD's flash memory.

facts.text: Without wear leveling, specific blocks would wear out early from repeated use, shortening the life of the whole drive.

The controller moves rarely changed (cold) data off heavily used blocks so frequently changing (hot) data can be written there; the extra writes are called write amplification and must be balanced against performance and durability.
A rewritten file generally lands in different NAND cells for wear leveling, and the file system need not manage wear leveling because the SSD handles it internally.
File systems that support SSDs generally support TRIM, which lets the SSD recycle discarded data and reduces garbage collection; log-structured file systems such as F2FS reduce write amplification.

definition.text: SSD endurance is how much writing a drive can take, listed on its datasheet as drive writes per day or as terabytes written.

facts.text: Drive writes per day (DWPD) is how many times the full capacity can be written per day within the warranty period, and terabytes written (TBW) is the total that can be written in that period; JEDEC standardizes both.
NAND lifespan is set by program-erase (P/E) cycles, and TBW is the product of the P/E cycle resource and the capacity: a 1 TB drive with TBW = 600 TB has 600 P/E cycles.
Once its rated terabytes written is reached, an SSD may lose data after three months (enterprise) or one year (consumer) without power, so SSDs are generally not suited to long-term archival storage.
SSDs also slow down as they approach full capacity.

conflicts.text: Heavily used consumer drives may start losing data typically after one to two years unpowered in storage.
conflicts.note: Same page, different condition and period; the table row on retention gives three months or one year once the nominal written life is reached.

definition.text: SSDs can serve as a fast cache layer in front of slower hard-disk-based storage.

facts.text: In a distributed environment an SSD layer can absorb the large volume of user requests to slower HDD-based storage, giving much higher bandwidth and lower latency than the storage system alone.
Such a layer can be managed as a distributed key-value database or a distributed file system, and on supercomputers it is called a burst buffer.
On one machine an SSD can cache a hard disk, either as a separate drive, as with bcache, dm-cache and Apple's Fusion Drive, or as flash built into a hybrid drive (SSHD).
In ZFS a low-latency SSD can hold the intent log (SLOG), and an SSD can serve as the level 2 read cache (L2ARC).

definition.text: A hard disk drive (HDD) is an electro-mechanical storage device that stores digital data magnetically on rapidly rotating platters.

facts.text: Magnetic heads on a moving actuator arm read and write the platters; access is random, so blocks can be stored and retrieved in any order, and the data persists when power is off.
Access time is limited by mechanics: seek time to move the head to the right track, rotational latency waiting for the sector to pass under the head, and the time to transfer the data.
Average rotational latency is half the rotational period: 4.16 ms at 7,200 rpm and 5.55 ms at 5,400 rpm.
Time to access data has not kept up with throughput increases, which have not kept up with growth in bit density and capacity.

HDDs cost much less per bit; SSDs cost four to nine times more per bit but replace HDDs where speed, power consumption, size and durability matter, while HDDs dominate the volume of server storage produced.

Drives store extra ECC bits per block, particularly Reed-Solomon, so many errors are corrected invisibly and denser recording is possible; a typical 1 TB disk with 512-byte sectors spends about 93 GB on ECC data.
Data is stored in logical blocks, each delimited by markers and carrying error detecting and correcting information; blocks often held 512 bytes of usable data.
To minimize cost and overcome failures of individual HDDs, storage providers rely on redundant HDD arrays and replace failed drives on an ongoing basis.

definition.text: Hard disks fail through mechanical damage and media errors, and drives combine error correction and sector remapping to hide most of them.

facts.text: In a head crash the head scrapes the platter and grinds away the magnetic film, losing data; causes include electronic or sudden power failure, physical shock, contamination, wear, corrosion and poor manufacture.
A drive remaps the data of a failing sector to a spare sector from a reserve pool while ECC can still recover it; S.M.A.R.T. counts ECC fixes and remappings but warns only of mechanical issues.

Uncorrected bit read error rates are specified at one in 10^16 bits for 2013 enterprise SAS drives and one in 10^14 for 2018 consumer SATA drives; silent corruptions, undetected by firmware or the operating system, are worst.
Studies find drive grade does not predict failure rate, failure rates rise steadily with age, and in drive arrays one drive's failure significantly raises the short-term risk of a second.

definition.text: Storage drives connect to a computer over bus interfaces such as ATA, SATA, SCSI, SAS and Fibre Channel.

facts.text: Hard drives connect over parallel ATA, Serial ATA, SCSI, Serial Attached SCSI (SAS) or Fibre Channel, and portable drives use USB or IEEE 1394; all are digital interfaces.
SAS is a serial protocol that still uses SCSI commands and is compatible with SATA, so a SAS controller can drive SATA drives but a SATA controller cannot drive SAS drives.
Fibre Channel succeeded parallel SCSI on the enterprise market and is the cornerstone of storage area networks, with iSCSI and ATA over Ethernet as newer alternatives.
SSDs use SATA (up to 6.0 Gbit/s for SATA 3.0), SAS (12.0 Gbit/s for SAS 3.0) or PCIe (31.5 Gbit/s for 3.0 x4); NVMe, built for SSDs, offers much lower latency and higher throughput than AHCI.

definition.text: Network File System (NFS) is a distributed file system protocol that lets a client computer access files over a network much like local storage.

facts.text: NFS builds on the ONC remote procedure call system, and every version after the first experimental one is defined in RFCs so anyone can implement it.
NFS version 2 (RFC 1094) originally ran only over UDP, and its designers meant the server side to be stateless, with locking implemented outside the core protocol.

NFSv2 reads only the first 2 GB of a file; NFSv3 added 64-bit file sizes and offsets, asynchronous server writes to ease slow synchronous writes, and READDIRPLUS to return attributes with directory listings.
TCP support arrived with NFSv3; TCP made NFS over a WAN more feasible and allowed transfer sizes beyond the 8 KB limit that UDP imposes.
NFSv4 (RFC 3010, revised in RFC 3530 and RFC 7530), influenced by AFS and SMB, adds performance improvements, mandates strong security and is a stateful protocol.
NFSv4 needs only one UDP or TCP port, 2049, which simplifies use across firewalls.

NFSv4.1 (RFC 5661, revised in RFC 8881) supports clustered servers with scalable parallel access to files spread over multiple servers (pNFS), and NFSv4.2 (RFC 7862) adds server-side clone and copy and sparse files.
NFS runs on Unix-like systems, Windows and others, though Windows and macOS default to SMB as their networking protocol.

definition.text: Parallel NFS (pNFS), part of NFSv4.1, separates file metadata from file data so a client can move data directly to and from a set of data servers.

facts.text: A traditional NFS server holds file names and their data together, while NFSv4.1 separates filesystem metadata from the location of file data and stripes the data among a set of data servers.

A pNFS server is a set of components controlled by a metadata server; the client contacts one metadata server to traverse the namespace but may interact directly with the data servers when moving data.

The NFSv4.1 client can take part in locating file data and avoid funnelling all transfers through one NFS server, whereas some multi-node NFS products give the client only a limited part in separating metadata from data.

definition.text: Server Message Block (SMB) is a communication protocol used to share files, printers, serial ports and other communications between nodes on a network.

facts.text: SMB enables file sharing, printer sharing, network browsing and inter-process communication; it relies on TCP and IP, with the server on TCP port 445, so it works across interconnected networks, including the Internet.

On Windows domain networks SMB authenticates users with Kerberos against Active Directory, on simpler peer-to-peer networks it uses NTLM, and messages can be digitally signed to prevent some man-in-the-middle attacks.
SMB 1.0 performs poorly over high-latency links because it is chatty, block-level rather than streaming, limited to a 64K block size and not tuned for WAN links.
SMB2 cuts chattiness by reducing commands from over a hundred to nineteen, pipelines requests before earlier responses arrive, and compounds multiple actions into one request to save round trips.
SMB 3.0 added SMB Direct (SMB over RDMA), SMB Multichannel (multiple connections per session) and end-to-end encryption, aimed at virtualized data centers.
SMB over QUIC, introduced in Windows Server 2022, tunnels SMB in TLS 1.3 over UDP port 443 instead of TCP port 445, as a secure alternative to a VPN for remote file access.
In 1996 Microsoft published SMB 1.0 as CIFS, which supports symbolic links, hard links and larger files but none of the features of SMB 2.0 and later; the CIFS name has since been dropped.
Samba is a free reimplementation of SMB that lets Unix-like systems interoperate with Windows as file and print server or client.

definition.text: An SMB opportunistic lock (OpLock) lets a client cache a network file locally to improve performance; it is not a true lock and gives no mutual exclusion.

facts.text: When a client opens a file that no one else has open, the server grants an exclusive OpLock, so the client may cache all changes locally and needs fewer round trips to read and write.

When another client opens the file, the server sends a break to revoke the OpLock; the first client flushes its changes and acknowledges, and only then does the server answer the second client consistently.
After a break the client may get a Level 2 OpLock, which allows caching reads but not writes, and batch OpLocks let a client delay its close for files opened and closed repeatedly.
A client holding an OpLock does not really hold a lock; it is notified by a break when another client wants incompatible access, and that client's request waits while the break is processed.

definition.text: iSCSI is an IP-based storage networking standard that provides block-level access to storage devices by carrying SCSI commands over a TCP/IP network.

facts.text: Clients, called initiators, send SCSI commands to storage devices, called targets, on remote servers; as a SAN protocol it lets organizations consolidate storage into arrays while clients such as database servers see locally attached SCSI disks.
iSCSI needs no dedicated cabling and runs over existing IP infrastructure, so it is seen as a low-cost alternative to Fibre Channel, which requires dedicated infrastructure except as FCoE.
An iSCSI SAN can be severely degraded if not run on a dedicated network or VLAN, because of competition for a fixed amount of bandwidth.

A LUN (logical unit number) is an individually addressable logical SCSI device within a target, essentially a numbered disk; in enterprise deployments LUNs usually represent subsets of large RAID arrays, often one per client.

Initiators treat LUNs like raw disks: rather than mounting remote directories as with NFS or CIFS, the host formats and manages a file system on the LUN, and iSCSI leaves sharing a LUN among computers to the operating system.

iSCSI SANs serve storage consolidation, where a server gets a new disk volume without hardware or cabling changes, and disaster recovery, mirroring storage to a remote data center that can act as a standby.

Software initiators, kernel drivers that use the existing network card, are the most common deployment; hardware initiators such as iSCSI HBAs offload TCP and iSCSI processing for better server performance at extra cost.

iSCSI runs over TCP (typically ports 860 and 3260) and mostly sends cleartext, so administrators usually run it on logically isolated networks or VLANs and authenticate initiators and targets with CHAP.

definition.text: Fibre Channel is a high-speed protocol providing in-order, lossless delivery of raw block data, used mainly to connect servers to storage in storage area networks.

facts.text: Its two major characteristics are in-order and lossless delivery of raw block data, with lossless delivery achieved through a credit mechanism.
Fibre Channel is primarily used to connect storage to servers in SANs in commercial data centers; a SAN is a dedicated network that lets multiple servers access data from one or more storage devices.
Fibre Channel Protocol (FCP) carries SCSI commands over Fibre Channel, FICON carries ESCON commands for IBM mainframes, and NVMe commands can be carried to reach flash storage.

There are three topologies: point-to-point; arbitrated loop, a ring where only one pair of ports communicates at a time and one device failure breaks the loop, rarely used after 2010; and switched fabric.

In a switched fabric every device connects to switches that route with Fabric Shortest Path First; it scales to tens of thousands of ports, many port pairs talk at once, and a port failure stays isolated to its link.
SANs are often designed with dual fabrics for fault tolerance: two completely separate fabrics run, and if the primary fails the second becomes primary.

Servers attach through host bus adapters (HBAs), each with a unique World Wide Name (WWN); a World Wide Node Name can be shared by ports of a device, while a World Wide Port Name is unique to each port.
Fibre Channel has five layers, from FC-0 (physical) to FC-4 (mapping of SCSI, NVMe, IP and FICON), rather than following the OSI model; data rates range from 1 to 128 gigabit per second.

definition.text: Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) is an AWS service that provides object storage through a web service interface.

facts.text: S3 aims to provide scalability, high availability and low latency with high durability, and stores any type of object for uses such as backups, disaster recovery, archives and data lakes for analytics.
Objects are the basic units and are organized into buckets; each object is identified by a unique, user-assigned key, and buckets are managed through the console, the AWS SDK or the REST API.
An object can be between 0 bytes and 5 TB; a single upload operation allows at most 5 GB, so larger objects must go through the multipart upload API.
Requests are authorized with an access control list on each bucket, versioning is disabled by default, and authenticated URLs can be created that are valid for a specified time.

S3 has nine storage classes with different durability, availability and performance; Standard is the default for frequently accessed data, while Express One Zone gives single-digit millisecond latency but keeps data in one availability zone.
A bucket can be mounted as a file system with FUSE-based tools, but S3 semantics are not those of a POSIX file system, so it may not behave entirely as expected.
As of 2025, S3 stores 500 trillion objects, 100s of exabytes of data, serves 200 million requests per second, and peaks at about 1 petabyte per second in bandwidth.
The broad adoption of the S3 API has produced S3-compatible storage from other providers and self-hostable open-source servers, including on-premises and private cloud deployments.

definition.text: Reed-Solomon codes are error-correcting codes, introduced by Irving Reed and Gustave Solomon in 1960, that treat a block of data as symbols of a finite field and add check symbols.

facts.text: An RS(n, k) code adds t = n - k check symbols to the data; it can detect up to t erroneous symbols, or locate and correct up to floor(t/2) erroneous symbols at unknown locations.
As an erasure code it can correct up to t erasures at known locations, and any mix of E errors and S erasures is correctable as long as 2E + S is at most n - k.
The code is maximum distance separable: its minimum distance n - k + 1 is the largest possible for a linear code of its size, known as the Singleton bound.
In the original view of Reed and Solomon, the message symbols are the coefficients of a polynomial of degree less than k, and the codeword is that polynomial's values at n distinct points.
Reed-Solomon codes suit burst errors because a symbol counts as one error however many of its bits are wrong; for random single-bit errors a binary code is usually the better choice.
Practical codes often use 8-bit symbols with 255 symbols per block; a common code carries 223 data symbols plus 32 parity symbols and corrects up to 16 symbol errors per block.
Reed-Solomon coding is widely used in mass storage systems to correct the burst errors from media defects, and in storage systems such as RAID 6.
The Cauchy-RS and Vandermonde-RS forms handle erasure channels: any K of the N codewords received are enough to reconstruct all N.

definition.text: In database systems, durability is the ACID guarantee that the effects of committed transactions survive permanently, even through failures and catastrophic events.

facts.text: A durable system tolerates three kinds of failure: transaction failures (an interrupted transaction), system failures (volatile storage lost in a crash) and media failures (loss of stable storage, typically disk failures).
To be durable, a database must make the effects of transactions committed before a failure survive, even by reconstruction, while the changes of incomplete transactions are reverted.

To survive the loss of volatile memory, the database flushes an immutable sequential log of transactions to non-volatile storage before acknowledging a commit; this logging mechanism is called a write-ahead log (WAL).

Because changes are logged before they modify database state, committed transactions can be redone from the log after a crash and incomplete ones undone, recreating the state right before the failure.

Systems differ in what they keep in volatile main memory: some hold all state and data there without durability, some keep part on non-volatile storage, others keep only state in memory and all data on disk, reflecting performance differences.
Against media failure, durability relies on stable memory built from replication and robust writing protocols, such as disk mirroring, so that even damaged storage hardware does not mean data loss.

Backup, data loss prevention and IT disaster recovery keep offline copies, and incremental dumps, differential files and checkpoints improve space and time compared with replaying every log file from the beginning.

In distributed databases all participating nodes must coordinate before a commit is acknowledged, usually by two-phase commit, and logging and recovery must handle distributed issues such as deadlocks; ARIES is a widely adopted family of recovery algorithms.
